n: Jesus learns that the Pharisees have heard He is gaining and baptizing more disciples than John. Growing attention from the authorities could bring conflict before His time.

f.w: made and baptized more disciples than John

n: John clarifies that Jesus Himself wasn’t personally baptizing — His disciples did, acting under His authority. The JST says Jesus baptized fewer than His disciples, letting them do it as an example.

f.g: JST John 4:3-4: “he himself baptized not so many as his disciples; for he suffered them for an example, preferring one another.”

n: So He leaves Judea and heads back north to Galilee.
He “had to” go through Samaria. It was the direct route, but many Jews detoured around it. John hints at a divine necessity — someone there needed Him.

f.g: Had to — perhaps a geographical and a divine necessity.
The central region between Judea and Galilee, home to the Samaritans.

n: He comes to Sychar, a Samaritan town near land Jacob had given his son Joseph centuries earlier.

f.g: Near ancient Shechem, at the foot of Mount Gerizim.

f.w: the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph

n: Jacob’s well is there. Tired from walking, Jesus sits by the well around noon — the hottest part of the day. The eternal Word truly shared human weariness.

f.g: A deep well still shown near Nablus today, more than 100 feet deep.
About noon.

n: A Samaritan woman comes to draw water. Jesus asks her for a drink. Women usually drew water in the cool morning or evening; coming at noon may suggest she was avoiding others.

f.g: By asking a favor, Jesus breaks social barriers and honors her.

n: His disciples have gone into town to buy food, leaving Jesus alone with her.

f.g: Food.

n: She is startled: You’re a Jew asking a Samaritan woman for a drink? Jews avoided Samaritans and even their dishes. Jesus crosses ethnic, religious, and gender lines.

f.w: the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans
f.g: Probably “Jews do not share vessels with Samaritans,” for fear of ritual impurity.

n: Jesus replies: if you knew God’s gift and who is asking you, you would have asked Him, and He would give you “living water.”

f.g: Common phrase for flowing spring water; Jesus uses it for the life He gives.

n: She takes Him literally: You have no bucket, and the well is deep. Where would you get this living water?

f.g: Travelers carried a leather bucket and rope.

n: Are You greater than our ancestor Jacob, who gave us this well? Ironically — yes, He is. Samaritans proudly claimed descent from Jacob through Joseph.

f.g: Samaritans claimed descent from the northern tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh.

n: Jesus points out that anyone who drinks this water will get thirsty again.

f.g: Earthly satisfactions never fully satisfy.

n: But the water He gives will satisfy forever, becoming a spring inside the person, bubbling up to eternal life. He speaks of the Spirit and the life He gives.

f.w: a well of water springing up into everlasting life

n: She asks for this water so she won’t be thirsty or have to keep coming to the well. She still thinks physically, but her heart is opening.

f.g: Her request is a step of faith, even if still misunderstood.

n: Jesus tells her to go call her husband and come back. He is gently opening the painful part of her life.

f.g: Jesus addresses the real need beneath her question.

n: She says she has no husband. Jesus replies: you’re right to say that.

f.g: You have spoken truly.

n: He reveals that she has had five husbands, and the man she lives with now isn’t her husband. He knows her completely — yet keeps talking with her, without condemning.

f.g: We are not told why — death, divorce, or both. Women could not easily initiate divorce then.

n: Astonished, she says: Sir, I can see You are a prophet.

f.g: Her understanding of Jesus keeps rising: a Jew, “Sir,” a prophet, then possibly the Christ.

n: She raises the great Jewish–Samaritan dispute: our ancestors worshipped on this mountain (Gerizim), but you Jews insist Jerusalem is the place to worship.

f.g: Mount Gerizim, where the Samaritans had a temple until the Jews destroyed it around 110 BC.

n: Jesus tells her a time is coming when worship of the Father won’t be tied to either place.

f.g: A respectful and earnest appeal.

n: Samaritans worshipped without fully understanding, accepting only the five books of Moses. Salvation comes through the Jews, for the Messiah descends from them.
The time has now come when true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and in truth. The Father seeks such worshippers.

f.g: With sincere hearts and in accordance with revealed truth.

f.w: the Father seeketh such to worship him

n: The KJV says “God is a Spirit.” The JST reads: “For unto such hath God promised his Spirit,” consistent with the Latter-day Saint teaching that the Father has a glorified body.

f.g: Greek has no “a” — “God is spirit.” JST John 4:26: “For unto such hath God promised his Spirit.”

n: She says she knows the Messiah is coming, and He will explain everything. Samaritans expected a figure they called the Taheb, “the one who returns” or restores.

f.g: Messiah.

f.w: he will tell us all things

n: Jesus answers plainly: I who speak to you am He. One of His clearest declarations of His identity is made to a Samaritan woman of questionable reputation.

f.w: I that speak unto thee am he
f.g: Greek egō eimi, “I am” — echoing the divine name.

n: The disciples return, surprised to find Him talking with a woman — rabbis typically didn’t speak with women in public. But no one dares question Him.

f.g: Were amazed.

n: The woman leaves her water jar behind — her original errand forgotten — and hurries into town to tell people.

f.g: A small detail showing she has found something more important.

n: Come see a man who told me everything I ever did! Could this be the Messiah? The woman who avoided people becomes a missionary to them.

f.g: Phrased as a hopeful question — inviting them to judge for themselves.

n: The townspeople leave the city and come out to Jesus.

f.g: In Greek, “were coming” — a stream of people approaching.

n: Meanwhile the disciples urge Him to eat.

f.g: Urged, asked Him.

n: He says He has food they don’t know about.

f.g: Food — here spiritual nourishment.

n: Puzzled, they ask each other whether someone brought Him food. Like the woman, they think only literally.

f.g: Anything (aught).

n: His food is doing the will of the One who sent Him and completing His work. Serving God nourishes Him more than bread.

f.w: My meat is to do the will of him that sent me

n: People say harvest is still four months away, but Jesus says look — the fields are already white for harvest. The Samaritans streaming toward them, perhaps in white clothing, are the harvest.
The reaper already receives wages, gathering a harvest for eternal life, so sower and reaper can rejoice together.
The saying is true: one plants, another harvests.
He sends them to reap what others planted. The prophets, John the Baptist, and now this woman prepared the ground; the disciples gather the fruit.
Many Samaritans in that town believe in Jesus because of the woman’s testimony: He told me everything I ever did.

f.w: believed on him for the saying of the woman
f.g: Her simple testimony was powerful.

n: They come and urge Him to stay, and He stays two days — a Jew lodging with Samaritans.

f.g: Stay.
Stayed.

n: Many more believe because of His own words.

f.g: Direct contact with Christ deepens faith begun through others.

n: They tell the woman: now we believe not just because of what you said, but because we’ve heard Him ourselves. He truly is the Savior of the world — not just of the Jews.

f.g: Testimony must become personal.

n: After two days, Jesus continues on to Galilee.

f.g: From there.

n: Jesus Himself had said a prophet isn’t honored in his own homeland — a principle that applies to His reception in Nazareth and Galilee.

f.w: a prophet hath no honour in his own country

n: The Galileans welcome Him because they had seen what He did at the Passover feast in Jerusalem. Their welcome is based on miracles.
He returns to Cana, where He had turned water to wine. A royal official whose son is ill in Capernaum hears He is there.

f.g: A royal official, probably serving Herod Antipas.

n: The official travels about twenty miles to find Jesus and begs Him to come heal his son, who is near death.

f.g: Capernaum lies lower, by the lake; Cana is in the hills.
Dying.

n: Jesus says: unless you people see signs and wonders, you won’t believe. He wants faith that rests on Him, not just on spectacle.
The father doesn’t argue — he just pleads: Sir, come before my child dies.

f.g: Before.

n: Jesus tells him: Go home; your son lives. The man believes the word alone and leaves. He shows the kind of faith Jesus is seeking — trusting His word without seeing.
On the way home, his servants meet him with the news: your son is alive!

f.g: The servants repeat Jesus’ exact words.

n: He asks when the boy began to improve. They say: yesterday at the seventh hour, the fever left him.

f.g: About 1 p.m.
Get better.

n: The father realizes it was the exact moment Jesus spoke. He and his whole household believe — his faith grows from trusting a word to full conversion.

f.g: His entire household — family and servants.

n: This was the second sign Jesus performed after returning from Judea to Galilee — both at Cana.

f.g: The second of John’s seven signs.
